slices.label: Men outside the South
slices.source: 1880 and 1890 censuses interpolated to November 1884; men 21+ outside the eleven Southern states (including declarant aliens where they could vote); turnout and choice from the backbone, calibrated to certified 1884 returns.

slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: 1880 and 1890 censuses interpolated to November 1884; women 21+ outside the South; no state let women vote for president in 1884 (women voted in Wyoming Territory, which had no electoral votes), so this slice casts no presidential vote.

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1880 and 1890 censuses interpolated to November 1884; white adults in the eleven former Confederate states (includes a small number of American Indian and Asian adults); calibrated to certified 1884 returns.

slices.label: Black Southerners
slices.source: 1880 and 1890 censuses interpolated to November 1884; Black adults in the eleven former Confederate states; Black men still voted in large numbers, but violence, fraud and laws like South Carolina's 1882 eight-box law cut their turnout; the shortfall against white turnout is counted as exclusion.

slices.label: Immigrants not yet citizens
slices.source: 1880 and 1890 censuses interpolated to November 1884; foreign-born white adults who were aliens or had only declared their intent (first papers); declarant aliens could vote in several Midwestern and Western states (fewer each decade as states repealed it), so part of this slice could vote.

whatIfs.assumption: Every adult votes. Non-citizens choose like naturalized citizens of their state and sex; Black Southerners like Black voters outside the South; everyone else as their group did in 1884.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1884 comes out as it did: Cleveland wins, 219–182. The closest state was New York, which went to Cleveland by 0.1 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1880 and 1890 census counts interpolated to 1884 and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1884 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

everyone.summary: 17.5 million more adults vote. California, Colorado, Florida, Iowa and 14 more flip, but Cleveland still wins, 343–58. The closest call is Nebraska, which holds for Blaine by 0.4 points. Blaine wins in 5 of 100 draws.

howIGotThis: What changed: Every adult can vote, and turns out.

south-white.name: Anna Reed
south-white.quote: My husband will vote tomorrow, but the law doesn't permit women like me to have a say in who leads the country.
south-white.controlQuote: My husband will vote tomorrow, but the law doesn't permit women like me to have a say in who leads the country.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: I cannot vote, though I hear the men are much concerned about the corruption question and the tariff. My husband will cast his ballot tomorrow.
women.controlQuote: I cannot vote, though I hear the men are much concerned about the corruption question and the tariff. My husband will cast his ballot tomorrow.

men.name: Ernest Reed
men.quote: The Republican's kept work steady and wages up these past years. I worry what lowering the tariff would do to the mills, but the man's got a point about corruption in Washington.
